questions.stem: What is the Harrod-Domar growth formula?
options: Growth rate = Savings ratio / Capital-output ratio
Growth rate = Capital-output ratio / Savings ratio
Growth rate = Savings ratio x Capital-output ratio
Growth rate = Investment / GDP
questions.why: Growth can be raised either by increasing the savings ratio or by using capital more efficiently, meaning a lower capital-output ratio.
whyNot: That inverts the formula.
The two are divided, not multiplied.
That is the investment ratio, one input to the model.

questions.stem: Which of the following best defines the savings gap?
options: The shortfall between savings available domestically and the investment needed for growth
The difference between planned and actual saving
The gap between the interest rate on savings and on loans
The shortfall in foreign exchange needed to buy imports
questions.why: Low income means most of it must be consumed, so the savings ratio is low, which is the circularity of the poverty trap.
whyNot: That is a disequilibrium in saving.
That is the interest rate spread.
That is the foreign currency gap.

questions.stem: Which of the following best defines the foreign currency gap?
options: A shortage of foreign exchange to pay for necessary imports and debt service
A shortage of domestic savings for investment
A difference between the official and market exchange rates
A shortage of foreign workers in an economy
questions.why: Capital equipment, fuel and technology must be imported, and that requires foreign currency, which debt service competes for directly.
whyNot: That is the savings gap.
That is a parallel market premium.
That is a labour shortage.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a non-economic constraint named in the specification?
options: Corruption
Volatility of commodity prices
The savings gap
Capital flight
questions.why: The five non-economic constraints are corruption, poor governance, civil wars, migration and terrorism.
whyNot: That is an economic constraint.
That is an economic constraint.
That is an economic constraint.

questions.stem: A savings ratio of 6% and a capital-output ratio of 4. What is the growth rate?
questions.why: 6 / 4 = 1.5% a year. With population growing at 2.2%, income per head would be falling.
whyNot: That multiplies rather than divides.
That inverts the formula.
That adds the two figures.

questions.stem: The savings ratio rises to 12% and the capital-output ratio falls to 3. What is the growth rate?
questions.why: 12 / 3 = 4.0%. Growth can be raised by more investment or by using capital more efficiently, and the second is cheaper.
whyNot: That uses a capital-output ratio of 4.
That uses the original savings ratio.
That multiplies the figures.

questions.stem: Why are commodity prices so volatile?
options: Both supply and demand are price inelastic in the short run, so a small shift moves price a lot
Supply and demand are both highly elastic
Governments fix commodity prices
Commodity markets have very few buyers
questions.why: Supply depends on harvests and long investment lead times; demand is derived or a necessity.
whyNot: Elastic curves would produce small price movements.
Most commodity prices are market determined.
Commodity markets typically have many participants.

questions.stem: Why is volatility a problem even when the average commodity price is adequate?
options: Export earnings and government revenue swing unpredictably, which makes planning impossible
Volatility reduces the average price over time
Volatility prevents any trade from occurring
Volatility only affects importers
questions.why: It also deters investment, because returns are unpredictable, and destabilises producers' incomes.
whyNot: Volatility concerns variation around the average.
Trade continues at fluctuating prices.
It affects exporters most directly.

questions.stem: What is the low value added problem in primary product dependency?
options: Exporting raw cocoa rather than chocolate means the processing profit and skilled jobs accrue elsewhere
Primary products cannot be sold at a profit
Primary products have no international market
Primary production requires no labour
questions.why: That is the argument for moving up the value chain rather than simply diversifying into other primary products.
whyNot: They are profitable, at volatile prices.
World markets for them are large.
It is often highly labour-intensive.

questions.stem: What is the strongest limitation of the Harrod-Domar model?
options: It assumes capital is the only constraint, when skills, institutions and infrastructure may bind harder
It cannot be calculated from available data
It ignores the savings ratio
It applies only to developed economies
questions.why: It also assumes investment is productive, which depends on governance, and ignores technology.
whyNot: The inputs are routinely estimated.
The savings ratio is its numerator.
It was developed with developing economies in mind.

options: The depreciation it causes prompts further outflows
It raises domestic interest rates permanently
It increases foreign exchange reserves
It attracts inward investment
questions.why: It also frequently coincides with inward aid, so the country loses private capital while receiving public transfers.
whyNot: Rates may rise in response, but that is not the self-reinforcement.
It depletes reserves.
It signals loss of confidence, which deters investment.

questions.stem: What is the demographic dividend, and what does realising it require?
options: A large working-age cohort supporting few dependants, requiring education and available jobs
A high birth rate raising total output automatically
An ageing population reducing the dependency ratio
Emigration reducing the size of the labour force
questions.why: Without the education and the jobs, the dividend becomes youth unemployment.
whyNot: A high birth rate raises the dependency ratio.
Ageing raises the dependency ratio.
Emigration reduces the workforce rather than creating a dividend.

questions.stem: Why is poor governance arguably the binding constraint on development?
options: It determines whether any of the economic remedies work: aid is stolen, investment stays away, taxes go uncollected
It is the easiest constraint to measure
It only affects the public sector
It has no effect on private investment
questions.why: Countries with similar resources and very different institutions have diverged enormously, which is the strongest evidence on this point.
whyNot: It is among the hardest to measure.
It affects contract enforcement and property rights throughout the economy.
Insecure property rights are a major deterrent to private investment.

questions.stem: Which of the following describes how constraints reinforce each other?
options: Debt service consumes the foreign currency needed to import the capital goods that would raise export earnings
Each constraint operates entirely independently
Removing one constraint removes all the others
Constraints only affect the public sector
questions.why: That interaction paragraph is the strongest available in a constraints essay, and few candidates write it.
whyNot: They interact, which is why poverty traps persist.
Removing the binding constraint helps; others remain.
They affect the whole economy.

questions.stem: Why does low education prevent technology transfer even when FDI arrives?
options: Without skills, workers and local firms cannot absorb and use the technology
Foreign investors are prohibited from training local staff
Technology cannot be used in developing economies
Education has no effect on productivity
questions.why: Education is the constraint whose removal loosens the most other constraints, which is why it is worth prioritising.
whyNot: Training is common and often required.
It is used widely where skills exist.
It is a direct determinant of productivity.

questions.stem: Why is infrastructure a particularly stubborn constraint?
options: It needs very large capital sums with long payback, which a country facing a savings gap cannot fund
Infrastructure is cheap and quick to build
Infrastructure has no effect on business costs
The private sector always provides it adequately
questions.why: It is also largely a public good, so private provision is inadequate, requiring a state with the revenue and competence to build it.
whyNot: It is expensive and slow.
Poor transport and power raise costs for every firm.
Non-excludability means under-provision.

questions.stem: Why is migration not purely a loss for a developing economy?
options: Remittances are large and reliable, returning migrants bring skills, and the prospect can raise enrolment in training
Emigration has no effect on the labour force
Skilled workers never emigrate
Remittances are recorded as aid
questions.why: The brain drain is real, and the offsetting effects mean the net position has to be judged rather than assumed.
whyNot: It reduces the labour force directly.
The brain drain concerns exactly those workers.
Remittances are secondary income on the current account.
